q1.answer: Na⁺ is charged but has no unpaired electron in its closed-shell ion. NH₄⁺ is charged and has no unpaired electron. Cl• is neutral and has one unpaired electron. [M]•⁺ is charged and has an unpaired electron: loss of one electron makes a radical cation. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different neutron numbers/masses. Ions differ in electron number and therefore charge.
rubric: Classifies charge and radical status for all four species.
Defines [M]•⁺ as a radical cation formed by electron loss.
Distinguishes isotope neutron/mass change from ion electron/charge change.
q1.explanation: The dot means an unpaired electron, not merely an electrical charge.

q2.answer: 34.969(1−y)+36.966y=35.45, so 1.997y=0.481 and y=0.241: about 24.1% ³⁷Cl and 75.9% ³⁵Cl. CH₂Cl₂ has discrete molecular-isotope masses 84 (³⁵Cl₂), 86 (³⁵Cl³⁷Cl), and 88 (³⁷Cl₂). Its average molecular mass is a weighted mean, so it is not one of those discrete molecular-ion masses/peaks.
rubric: Sets up and solves the weighted-average equation to about 0.241.
Reports approximately 24% ³⁷Cl.
Names 84, 86, and 88 as the discrete CH₂Cl₂ isotope masses.
Explains why a weighted average is not an MS peak.
q2.explanation: A periodic-table average mass summarizes a population; MS resolves individual isotope combinations.

q3.answer: √(436×155)=√67580=260.0 kJ/mol. Δ=565−260=305 kJ/mol. Δχ=0.102√305=0.102(17.46)=1.78. Breaking H–F requires energy to overcome the attractive bond, so ΔH>0. Bond formation creates that attraction and releases energy, so ΔH<0.
rubric: Calculates the geometric mean near 260 and Δ near 305 kJ/mol.
Obtains Δχ about 1.78.
Correctly assigns positive ΔH to breaking and negative ΔH to forming with an energy explanation.
q3.explanation: BDE is defined for homolytic bond breaking in the gas phase.

q4.answer: m/z 70 is M and 71 is M+1. The M+1/M ratio is 5.5%, so carbon count is about 5. Formula C₅H₁₀ has mass 70 and is chemically valid. DoU=(2(5)+2−10)/2=1. It could be an alkene or a cycloalkane; the spectrum alone does not choose between those structural classes.
rubric: Identifies 70 as M and 71 as M+1.
Uses 1.1% per carbon to estimate five carbons.
Proposes C₅H₁₀ and calculates DoU=1.
Names an alkene or cycloalkane and avoids treating the formula as a unique structure.
q4.explanation: An M+1 peak estimates carbon count; it does not fully determine connectivity.

q5.answer: The arrow is Hδ+ → Clδ−. δ=(1.08×3.336×10⁻²⁰)/(1.602×10⁻¹⁹×1.27)=3.60×10⁻²⁰/2.03×10⁻¹⁹≈0.18, or about 18% ionic character. This is partial charge from unequal sharing, not transfer of a full electron to make H⁺ and Cl⁻; HCl is polar covalent.
rubric: Points the bond dipole from H toward Cl and labels partial charges.
Calculates δ≈0.18.
Interprets it as partial ionic character rather than full ionic charge.
q5.explanation: The course dipole-arrow convention runs from δ+ to δ−.

q6.answer: The best-supported class is a carboxylic acid: very broad acid O–H plus C=O and C–O. An ester has C=O and C–O but no O–H, so it cannot explain the exceptionally broad 2500–3300 cm⁻¹ feature. Hydrogen bonding makes each acid O–H experience a slightly different environment, broadening the band.
rubric: Identifies carboxylic acid.
Uses all three observed regions as support.
Rules out ester specifically by its missing O–H.
Links broadness to hydrogen-bonded environments.
q6.explanation: IR identification is strongest when multiple features agree and incompatible alternatives are eliminated.

q7.answer: n+1 gives the number of split lines within one signal, based on neighboring H; it does not count distinct environments/signals. (CH₃)₂CHBr has two environments: equivalent methyl H (6H) and one methine H (1H). Each methyl signal is a doublet from the one neighboring methine H. The methine signal is a septet from six equivalent neighboring methyl H.
rubric: Corrects signal counting versus split-line counting.
Gives two environments with 6H and 1H integration.
Gives methyl doublet and methine septet with correct neighbor counts.
q7.explanation: Symmetry is used before n+1; all six methyl hydrogens are equivalent neighbors of the methine proton.

q8.answer: Highest to lowest chemical shift: CH₂F > middle CH₂ > terminal CH₃. F withdraws electron density inductively; the effect weakens through successive σ bonds. The CH₂ nearest F is least shielded, so it feels more of the external field and resonates farther downfield/higher ppm. More distant environments retain more shielding.
rubric: Ranks CH₂F, middle CH₂, CH₃ in the correct order.
States induction decreases with distance.
Connects withdrawal to less shielding and higher ppm.
q8.explanation: Chemical shift is about the local electronic environment rather than simply the number of hydrogens.

q9.answer: 1-Octanol is more soluble in hexane: although its OH can hydrogen-bond with water, the long eight-carbon nonpolar tail dominates and has strong London compatibility with hexane. Choose GC because it has a polar liquid stationary phase and a gas carrier; hexane exits first because it has much weaker affinity for that polar phase than 1-butanol.
rubric: Selects hexane for greater 1-octanol solubility and explains the dominant long tail.
Chooses GC for the specified polar stationary phase.
Assigns hexane as earlier eluting and justifies using phase affinity.
q9.explanation: Like-with-like should be applied to the dominant features of both analyte and phase.

q10.answer: A 1:1 M:M+2 pair indicates one Br. C₃H₇Br fits M=122 for ⁷⁹Br (36+7+79=122), and m/z 43 is C₃H₇⁺ after loss of Br. The C–Br bond is weak, so this fragmentation is plausible; only the charged alkyl fragment is observed. ¹H NMR is the next measurement: read number of signals (environments/symmetry), chemical shift (induction/shielding), integration (H count), and splitting (neighbors).
rubric: Identifies one bromine from 1:1 M:M+2.
Proposes C₃H₇Br and checks mass 122.
Assigns m/z 43 as C₃H₇⁺ and relates it to weak C–Br cleavage.
Chooses ¹H NMR and names signal count, shift, integration, and splitting evidence.
q10.explanation: This follows the course pipeline: isotope evidence narrows formula, fragmentation supports a weak bond, and NMR tests environments/connectivity.
